Obtained
ŏb-tānd'
v. (past of obtain; in Scripture what the elect receive and the seeker does not — mercy got, not achieved)
From Latin obtinere — ob- (toward, against) plus tenere (to hold): literally to hold on to, to get and keep. The Latin carries a note of holding what one has come into possession of, which suits the biblical use exactly.

Biblical Definition

Obtained is one of the New Testament's quiet Calvinist words. Paul states the doctrine of election in a single line built on it: “Israel hath not obtained that which he seeketh for; but the election hath obtained it, and the rest were blinded” (Rom 11:7) — the seeking did not secure it and the election did. Peter says the same of the church made out of no people: “which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy” (1Pe 2:10), echoing Hosea's Lo-ruhamah. Hebrews uses it of what Christ secured by His own blood, and the tense matters: “by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us” (Heb 9:12) — the redemption is not offered as a possibility to be actualised by the sinner; it is obtained, done, held. And the same epistle turns the word toward the believer's daily need at the throne of grace: “that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need” (Heb 4:16). What was obtained once is obtained again every morning.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines obtain as to get, procure, or gain possession of, by effort or by request — noting that it implies coming into possession, however the thing is come by.

expand to see more

OBTAIN, v.t. To get; to gain; to procure; in a general sense, to gain possession of a thing, whether by effort, by request, or by gift.

That we may obtain mercy. Heb. iv.

2. To keep; to hold.

OBTAIN, v.i. To be received in customary or common use; to continue in use; as, the custom obtains.

Note. From the Latin obtineo, ob and teneo, to hold.

Key Scripture

Rom 11:7 — "What then? Israel hath not obtained that which he seeketh for; but the election hath obtained it, and the rest were blinded"

Heb 9:12 — "Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us."

1Pe 2:10 — "Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God: which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy."

Heb 4:16 — "Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need."

Modern Corruption

Heb 9:12 is read as though Christ obtained a redemption merely available to all, when the verb says He secured it — the difference between a purchased people and a possible one.

expand to see more

The universalising reading of the atonement holds that Christ's death made all men savable and that the sinner's faith converts the possibility into a fact. Heb 9:12 does not describe a possibility. Christ entered the holy place having obtained eternal redemption — an aorist participle reporting a completed acquisition — and He entered once, so nothing remains to be added. This is the doctrine of definite atonement, which Owen argued in The Death of Death: Christ did not die to make men redeemable but to redeem them, and what He purchased He will certainly have.

Rom 11:7 states the same principle on the human side, and it is a hard verse for every synergistic scheme. Israel sought and did not obtain; the election obtained. If seeking secured the thing, the seekers would have had it. Paul's conclusion is not that God is arbitrary but that mercy is mercy — “so then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16). And Heb 4:16 keeps the doctrine from ever becoming cold: the throne of a God who obtains for His people is the throne a believer may approach boldly, and obtain mercy again today.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin obtinere, to hold on to; rendering Greek epitugchano (G2013), to attain, eleeo (G1653) in the passive, to be shewn mercy, and heurisko (G2147) with the middle in Heb 9:12.

expand to see more

Latin obtinere — ob- + tenere, to hold; to come into and keep possession.

Greek epetuchen (from G2013) — “obtained” in Rom 11:7; to hit the mark, attain the thing aimed at.

Greek eleethentes (from G1653) — “having obtained mercy” (1Pe 2:10); a passive — mercy is received, never achieved.

Greek heuramenos (middle of G2147) — “having obtained” in Heb 9:12; the middle voice makes it a securing for Himself and for His people.

Hos 1:6, 10; 2:23 — Lo-ruhamah, “not having obtained mercy”, the prophecy Peter and Paul both apply to the calling of the Gentiles.

Usage

"“The election hath obtained it” — seeking did not secure it; election did."

"“Having obtained eternal redemption for us” — secured, not merely offered."

"“That we may obtain mercy” — the throne of grace approached boldly, today."
